# A simple tensor characteristic-function goodness-of-fit test

The function below compares the empirical characteristic function with the
characteristic function of a fitted tensor-variate normal or tensor-variate
skewed $t$ model. Its statistic is

\[
T_n = \frac{n}{L}\sum_{j=1}^L
\left|\widehat\varphi_n(t_j)-\varphi(t_j;\widehat\theta)\right|^2,
\]

where $L$ is the number of randomly selected frequency vectors. The p-value
is computed with a parametric bootstrap. Each bootstrap sample is re-fitted,
which accounts for using the same data to estimate the model and assess its
fit. A small `B` is useful while experimenting; use at least `B = 999` for a
reported analysis.

```{r simple-gof-test}
# Return matrices W_k for which W_k Sigma_k W_k' = I.
# Applying these matrices mode by mode standardizes the covariance without
# constructing a potentially enormous Kronecker covariance matrix.
.gof_whitening_matrices <- function(sigmas) {
  whitening <- vector("list", length(sigmas))

  for (k in seq_along(sigmas)) {
    sigma_k <- as.matrix(sigmas[[k]])
    sigma_k <- (sigma_k + t(sigma_k)) / 2
    chol_k <- chol(sigma_k)
    whitening[[k]] <- solve(t(chol_k))
  }

  whitening
}

# Center and whiten every tensor draw, then place the vectorized draws in an
# n by p matrix. Here p is the number of entries in one tensor draw.
.gof_standardize_draws <- function(draws, fit) {
  n <- n_draws(draws)
  p <- prod(draw_shape(draws))
  whitening <- .gof_whitening_matrices(fit$sigmas)
  standardized <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = p)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    current_draw <- pull_draw(draws, i) - fit$mu

    for (k in seq_along(whitening)) {
      current_draw <- n_prod(current_draw, k, whitening[[k]])
    }

    standardized[i, ] <- as.numeric(unclass(current_draw))
  }

  standardized
}

# Characteristic function of the standardized skewed t distribution.
# If W ~ InvGamma(nu/2, nu/2), then the standardized model is
# Z = W * a + sqrt(W) * epsilon, where epsilon ~ N(0, I).
.gof_skewt_cf <- function(frequencies, whitened_skew, nu) {
  number_frequencies <- nrow(frequencies)
  cf_values <- complex(number_frequencies)
  a <- nu / 2
  b <- nu / 2

  for (j in seq_len(number_frequencies)) {
    frequency <- frequencies[j, ]
    q <- sum(frequency^2)
    r <- sum(frequency * whitened_skew)
    s <- q / 2 - 1i * r

    # The CF equals one at the zero frequency.
    if (Mod(s) < .Machine$double.eps^0.5) {
      cf_values[j] <- 1 + 0i
    } else {
      # E[exp(-s W)] for an inverse-gamma W. The exponentially scaled
      # Bessel function is used to reduce numerical underflow.
      bessel_argument <- 2 * sqrt(b * s)
      log_cf <- log(2) +
        (a / 2) * (log(b) + log(s)) -
        lgamma(a) +
        log(Bessel::BesselK(
          bessel_argument,
          nu = a,
          expon.scaled = TRUE
        )) -
        bessel_argument

      cf_values[j] <- exp(log_cf)
    }
  }

  cf_values
}

# Create a function that evaluates the fitted standardized model CF.
.gof_make_model_cf <- function(model, fit) {
  if (model == "normal") {
    return(function(frequencies) {
      number_frequencies <- nrow(frequencies)
      cf_values <- complex(number_frequencies)

      for (j in seq_len(number_frequencies)) {
        cf_values[j] <- exp(-sum(frequencies[j, ]^2) / 2)
      }

      cf_values
    })
  }

  if (model == "skewt") {
    whitening <- .gof_whitening_matrices(fit$sigmas)
    whitened_skew <- fit$skew

    for (k in seq_along(whitening)) {
      whitened_skew <- n_prod(whitened_skew, k, whitening[[k]])
    }

    whitened_skew <- as.numeric(whitened_skew)

    return(function(frequencies) {
      .gof_skewt_cf(
        frequencies = frequencies,
        whitened_skew = whitened_skew,
        nu = fit$nu
      )
    })
  }

  # The multiscale CF helper already implements the remaining normal
  # variance-mean mixtures after modewise whitening.
  if (model %in% c("vargamma", "invgauss", "genhyper")) {
    return(function(frequencies) {
      .multiscale_cf_model(
        frequencies = frequencies,
        model = model,
        fit = fit
      )
    })
  }

  stop("No characteristic function is available for model `", model, "`.",
       call. = FALSE)
}

# Compute T_n for one data set and an already fitted model.
.gof_cf_statistic <- function(draws, model, fit, frequencies) {
  standardized <- .gof_standardize_draws(draws, fit)
  number_frequencies <- nrow(frequencies)
  empirical_cf <- complex(number_frequencies)

  # Compute the empirical CF separately at each frequency.
  for (j in seq_len(number_frequencies)) {
    phases <- standardized %*% frequencies[j, ]
    empirical_cf[j] <- mean(exp(1i * phases))
  }

  model_cf <- .gof_make_model_cf(model, fit)
  theoretical_cf <- model_cf(frequencies)

  differences <- empirical_cf - theoretical_cf
  statistic <- n_draws(draws) * mean(Mod(differences)^2)

  list(
    statistic = statistic,
    empirical_cf = empirical_cf,
    theoretical_cf = theoretical_cf
  )
}

# Compute the known-parameter covariance matrix of the cosine and sine CF
# features. Product-to-sum identities let us calculate every entry using CF
# values at sums and differences of the original frequencies.
.gof_feature_covariance <- function(frequencies, model, fit) {
  number_frequencies <- nrow(frequencies)
  number_features <- 2 * number_frequencies
  model_cf <- .gof_make_model_cf(model, fit)

  phi <- model_cf(frequencies)
  feature_mean <- c(Re(phi), Im(phi))
  second_moment <- matrix(
    0,
    nrow = number_features,
    ncol = number_features
  )

  for (j in seq_len(number_frequencies)) {
    for (k in seq_len(number_frequencies)) {
      frequency_plus <- frequencies[j, ] + frequencies[k, ]
      frequency_j_minus_k <- frequencies[j, ] - frequencies[k, ]
      frequency_k_minus_j <- -frequency_j_minus_k

      pair_frequencies <- rbind(
        frequency_plus,
        frequency_j_minus_k,
        frequency_k_minus_j
      )
      pair_cf <- model_cf(pair_frequencies)

      phi_plus <- pair_cf[1]
      phi_j_minus_k <- pair_cf[2]
      phi_k_minus_j <- pair_cf[3]

      # cos(A) cos(B) = {cos(A-B) + cos(A+B)} / 2
      second_moment[j, k] <-
        Re(phi_j_minus_k + phi_plus) / 2

      # sin(A) sin(B) = {cos(A-B) - cos(A+B)} / 2
      second_moment[number_frequencies + j,
                    number_frequencies + k] <-
        Re(phi_j_minus_k - phi_plus) / 2

      # cos(A) sin(B) = {sin(A+B) + sin(B-A)} / 2
      second_moment[j, number_frequencies + k] <-
        Im(phi_plus + phi_k_minus_j) / 2
      second_moment[number_frequencies + k, j] <-
        second_moment[j, number_frequencies + k]
    }
  }

  feature_covariance <- second_moment - tcrossprod(feature_mean)

  # Remove tiny asymmetry caused by floating-point calculations.
  (feature_covariance + t(feature_covariance)) / 2
}


# Perform the complete parameter-adjusted eigenvalue GOF test.
#
# If `fit` is supplied, it should be the model fitted to these same draws.
# Supplying true parameters would incorrectly apply a fitted-parameter
# correction; use the known-parameter eigenvalue test for that situation.
gof_test_eigenvalues_adjusted <- function(
    draws,
    model = c(
      "normal",
      "skewt",
      "vargamma",
      "invgauss",
      "genhyper"
    ),
    fit = NULL,
    freqs = NULL,
    n_frequencies = 20L,
    n_mixture = 100000L,
    frequency_sd = NULL,
    max_iter = 1000L,
    tol = 1e-6,
    quiet = TRUE,
    restrict = NULL,
    finite_difference = 1e-5,
    information_tolerance = 1e-8,
    eigen_tolerance = 1e-10,
    seed = NULL) {

  model <- match.arg(model)
  data_name <- deparse(substitute(draws))

  if (!inherits(draws, "tensor")) {
    stop("`draws` must be a tensor object.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (n_draws(draws) < 2L) {
    stop("At least two tensor draws are required.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (!is.null(seed)) {
    set.seed(seed)
  }

  p <- prod(draw_shape(draws))

  if (is.null(freqs)) {
    if (length(n_frequencies) != 1L ||
        !is.finite(n_frequencies) ||
        n_frequencies < 1L ||
        n_frequencies != floor(n_frequencies)) {
      stop("`n_frequencies` must be one positive integer.",
           call. = FALSE)
    }

    n_frequencies <- as.integer(n_frequencies)

    if (is.null(frequency_sd)) {
      frequency_sd <- 1 / sqrt(p)
    }

    freqs <- matrix(
      rnorm(
        n = n_frequencies * p,
        sd = frequency_sd
      ),
      nrow = n_frequencies,
      ncol = p
    )
  } else if (inherits(freqs, "tensor")) {
    if (!identical(
      as.integer(draw_shape(freqs)),
      as.integer(draw_shape(draws))
    )) {
      stop("The frequency tensors must have the same shape as the draws.",
           call. = FALSE)
    }

    freqs <- matrix(
      unclass(freqs),
      nrow = n_draws(freqs),
      ncol = p
    )
  } else {
    freqs <- as.matrix(freqs)

    if (ncol(freqs) != p || nrow(freqs) < 1L ||
        any(!is.finite(freqs))) {
      stop(
        "`freqs` must have one row per frequency and ",
        p,
        " finite columns.",
        call. = FALSE
      )
    }
  }

  if (length(n_mixture) != 1L ||
      !is.finite(n_mixture) ||
      n_mixture < 1L ||
      n_mixture != floor(n_mixture)) {
    stop("`n_mixture` must be one positive integer.",
         call. = FALSE)
  }

  n_mixture <- as.integer(n_mixture)

  if (is.null(fit)) {
    fit <- tensor_mle(
      draws,
      model = model,
      max_iter = max_iter,
      tol = tol,
      quiet = quiet,
      restrict = restrict
    )
  }

  observed <- .gof_cf_statistic(
    draws = draws,
    model = model,
    fit = fit,
    frequencies = freqs
  )

  adjusted <- compute_eigen_adjusted(
    draws = draws,
    freqs = freqs,
    model = model,
    fit = fit,
    max_iter = max_iter,
    tol = tol,
    quiet = quiet,
    restrict = restrict,
    finite_difference = finite_difference,
    information_tolerance = information_tolerance,
    eigen_tolerance = eigen_tolerance,
    return_details = TRUE
  )

  eigenvalues <- adjusted$eigenvalues
  mixture_statistics <- numeric(n_mixture)

  for (j in seq_along(eigenvalues)) {
    mixture_statistics <- mixture_statistics +
      eigenvalues[j] * rchisq(n_mixture, df = 1)
  }

  p_value <- (
    1 + sum(mixture_statistics >= observed$statistic)
  ) / (
    n_mixture + 1
  )

  model_label <- switch(
    model,
    normal = "tensor-variate normal",
    skewt = "tensor-variate skewed t",
    vargamma = "tensor-variate variance-gamma",
    invgauss = "tensor-variate inverse-Gaussian",
    genhyper = "tensor-variate generalized hyperbolic"
  )

  structure(
    list(
      statistic = c(T = observed$statistic),
      parameter = c(
        rank = length(eigenvalues),
        information_rank = adjusted$information_rank
      ),
      p.value = p_value,
      method = paste(
        "Parameter-adjusted eigenvalue CF goodness-of-fit test for the",
        model_label
      ),
      data.name = data_name,
      model = model,
      fit = fit,
      frequencies = freqs,
      empirical_cf = observed$empirical_cf,
      theoretical_cf = observed$theoretical_cf,
      adjusted_feature_covariance =
        adjusted$adjusted_feature_covariance,
      unadjusted_feature_covariance =
        adjusted$unadjusted_feature_covariance,
      parameter_correction = adjusted$parameter_correction,
      eigenvalues = eigenvalues,
      all_eigenvalues = adjusted$all_eigenvalues,
      information = adjusted$information,
      information_eigenvalues =
        adjusted$information_eigenvalues,
      information_rank = adjusted$information_rank,
      number_parameters = adjusted$number_parameters,
      parameter_names = adjusted$parameter_names,
      mean_score = adjusted$mean_score,
      n_mixture = n_mixture,
      parameters_treated_as_known = FALSE
    ),
    class = "htest"
  )
}

#' Characteristic-function goodness-of-fit test for tensor data
#'
#' @param draws A tensor object containing IID tensor draws.
#' @param model Either "normal" or "skewt".
#' @param B Number of parametric bootstrap samples. Use 999 or more for a
#'   reported analysis.
#' @param n_frequencies Number of characteristic-function frequencies.
#' @param frequency_sd Standard deviation used to generate each frequency
#'   coordinate. The default keeps frequency norms near one as p increases.
#' @param max_iter,tol,quiet,restrict Arguments passed to tensor_mle().
#' @param seed Optional random-number seed for reproducibility.
#'
#' @return An htest object containing the statistic and bootstrap p-value.
gof_test <- function(draws,
                     model = c("normal", "skewt"),
                     B = 199L,
                     n_frequencies = 20L,
                     frequency_sd = NULL,
                     max_iter = 1000L,
                     tol = 1e-4,
                     quiet = TRUE,
                     restrict = NULL,
                     seed = NULL) {
  model <- match.arg(model)
  data_name <- deparse(substitute(draws))

  if (!inherits(draws, "tensor")) {
    stop("`draws` must be a tensor object.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (n_draws(draws) < 2L) {
    stop("At least two tensor draws are required.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (length(B) != 1L || !is.finite(B) || B < 1 || B != floor(B)) {
    stop("`B` must be one positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (length(n_frequencies) != 1L || !is.finite(n_frequencies) ||
      n_frequencies < 1 || n_frequencies != floor(n_frequencies)) {
    stop("`n_frequencies` must be one positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  B <- as.integer(B)
  n_frequencies <- as.integer(n_frequencies)

  if (!is.null(seed)) {
    set.seed(seed)
  }

  n <- n_draws(draws)
  p <- prod(draw_shape(draws))

  if (is.null(frequency_sd)) {
    frequency_sd <- 1 / sqrt(p)
  }

  # Use one fixed frequency matrix for the observed statistic and every
  # bootstrap statistic. This ensures that they are directly comparable.
  frequencies <- matrix(
    rnorm(n_frequencies * p, sd = frequency_sd),
    nrow = n_frequencies,
    ncol = p
  )

  # Fit the requested null model to the observed draws.
  observed_fit <- tensor_mle(
    draws,
    model = model,
    max_iter = max_iter,
    tol = tol,
    quiet = quiet,
    restrict = restrict
  )

  observed <- .gof_cf_statistic(
    draws = draws,
    model = model,
    fit = observed_fit,
    frequencies = frequencies
  )

  bootstrap_statistics <- numeric(B)

  # Generate samples from the fitted model. Crucially, each bootstrap sample
  # is re-fitted before its statistic is computed.
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    if (model == "normal") {
      bootstrap_draws <- rtnorm(
        n = n,
        mu = observed_fit$mu,
        sigmas = observed_fit$sigmas
      )
    } else {
      bootstrap_draws <- rtskewt(
        n = n,
        mu = observed_fit$mu,
        sigmas = observed_fit$sigmas,
        skew = observed_fit$skew,
        nu = observed_fit$nu
      )
    }

    bootstrap_fit <- tensor_mle(
      bootstrap_draws,
      model = model,
      max_iter = max_iter,
      tol = tol,
      quiet = quiet,
      restrict = restrict
    )

    bootstrap_result <- .gof_cf_statistic(
      draws = bootstrap_draws,
      model = model,
      fit = bootstrap_fit,
      frequencies = frequencies
    )

    bootstrap_statistics[b] <- bootstrap_result$statistic
  }

  # The add-one formula prevents a bootstrap p-value of exactly zero.
  p_value <- (1 + sum(bootstrap_statistics >= observed$statistic)) /
    (B + 1)

  method_name <- if (model == "normal") {
    "Bootstrap CF goodness-of-fit test for the tensor-variate normal"
  } else {
    "Bootstrap CF goodness-of-fit test for the tensor-variate skewed t"
  }

  structure(
    list(
      statistic = c(T = observed$statistic),
      parameter = c(B = B),
      p.value = p_value,
      method = method_name,
      data.name = data_name,
      fit = observed_fit,
      frequencies = frequencies,
      empirical_cf = observed$empirical_cf,
      theoretical_cf = observed$theoretical_cf,
      bootstrap_statistics = bootstrap_statistics
    ),
    class = "htest"
  )
}

#' Eigenvalue CF goodness-of-fit test for tensor data
#'
#' This faster version treats the fitted parameters as if they were known. It
#' does not generate tensor bootstrap samples or re-fit the model. Instead, it
#' approximates the null distribution by a weighted sum of chi-squares:
#'
#'     lambda_1 * chi-square_1 + ... + lambda_r * chi-square_1.
#'
#' @param draws A tensor object containing IID tensor draws.
#' @param model Either "normal" or "skewt".
#' @param n_frequencies Number of characteristic-function frequencies.
#' @param n_mixture Number of draws from the weighted chi-squared limit used
#'   to calculate the p-value. These are inexpensive scalar simulations.
#' @param frequency_sd Standard deviation used to generate each frequency
#'   coordinate. The default keeps frequency norms near one as p increases.
#' @param eigen_tolerance Relative cutoff for retaining positive eigenvalues.
#' @param max_iter,tol,quiet,restrict Arguments passed to tensor_mle().
#' @param seed Optional random-number seed for reproducibility.
#'
#' @return An htest object containing the statistic, eigenvalues, and p-value.
gof_test_eigenvalues <- function(draws,
                                 model = c("normal", "skewt"),
                                 n_frequencies = 20L,
                                 n_mixture = 100000L,
                                 frequency_sd = NULL,
                                 eigen_tolerance = 1e-10,
                                 max_iter = 1000L,
                                 tol = 1e-4,
                                 quiet = TRUE,
                                 restrict = NULL,
                                 seed = NULL) {
  model <- match.arg(model)
  data_name <- deparse(substitute(draws))

  if (!inherits(draws, "tensor")) {
    stop("`draws` must be a tensor object.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (n_draws(draws) < 2L) {
    stop("At least two tensor draws are required.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (length(n_frequencies) != 1L || !is.finite(n_frequencies) ||
      n_frequencies < 1 || n_frequencies != floor(n_frequencies)) {
    stop("`n_frequencies` must be one positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (length(n_mixture) != 1L || !is.finite(n_mixture) ||
      n_mixture < 1 || n_mixture != floor(n_mixture)) {
    stop("`n_mixture` must be one positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (length(eigen_tolerance) != 1L || !is.finite(eigen_tolerance) ||
      eigen_tolerance <= 0) {
    stop("`eigen_tolerance` must be one positive number.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  n_frequencies <- as.integer(n_frequencies)
  n_mixture <- as.integer(n_mixture)

  if (!is.null(seed)) {
    set.seed(seed)
  }

  p <- prod(draw_shape(draws))

  if (is.null(frequency_sd)) {
    frequency_sd <- 1 / sqrt(p)
  }

  frequencies <- matrix(
    rnorm(n_frequencies * p, sd = frequency_sd),
    nrow = n_frequencies,
    ncol = p
  )

  # This is the only model fit required by the eigenvalue method.
  fit <- tensor_mle(
    draws,
    model = model,
    max_iter = max_iter,
    tol = tol,
    quiet = quiet,
    restrict = restrict
  )

  observed <- .gof_cf_statistic(
    draws = draws,
    model = model,
    fit = fit,
    frequencies = frequencies
  )

  feature_covariance <- .gof_feature_covariance(
    frequencies = frequencies,
    model = model,
    fit = fit
  )

  # Because T_n divides the squared CF differences by L, its limiting
  # chi-squared weights are the eigenvalues of V / L.
  eigen_result <- eigen(
    feature_covariance / n_frequencies,
    symmetric = TRUE,
    only.values = TRUE
  )
  all_eigenvalues <- eigen_result$values
  largest_eigenvalue <- max(all_eigenvalues, 0)
  cutoff <- largest_eigenvalue * eigen_tolerance
  eigenvalues <- all_eigenvalues[all_eigenvalues > cutoff]

  if (length(eigenvalues) == 0L) {
    stop("The feature covariance has numerical rank zero.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  # This simulation uses scalar chi-squares only. It does not simulate tensor
  # data and does not call tensor_mle() again.
  mixture_statistics <- numeric(n_mixture)

  for (j in seq_along(eigenvalues)) {
    mixture_statistics <- mixture_statistics +
      eigenvalues[j] * rchisq(n_mixture, df = 1)
  }

  # The add-one formula prevents a simulated p-value of exactly zero.
  p_value <- (1 + sum(mixture_statistics >= observed$statistic)) /
    (n_mixture + 1)

  method_name <- if (model == "normal") {
    paste(
      "Eigenvalue CF goodness-of-fit test for the tensor-variate normal",
      "(fitted parameters treated as known)"
    )
  } else {
    paste(
      "Eigenvalue CF goodness-of-fit test for the tensor-variate skewed t",
      "(fitted parameters treated as known)"
    )
  }

  structure(
    list(
      statistic = c(T = observed$statistic),
      parameter = c(rank = length(eigenvalues)),
      p.value = p_value,
      method = method_name,
      data.name = data_name,
      fit = fit,
      frequencies = frequencies,
      empirical_cf = observed$empirical_cf,
      theoretical_cf = observed$theoretical_cf,
      feature_covariance = feature_covariance,
      eigenvalues = eigenvalues,
      all_eigenvalues = all_eigenvalues,
      n_mixture = n_mixture,
      parameters_treated_as_known = TRUE
    ),
    class = "htest"
  )
}
```


```{r eigenvalue-gof-test-example}
normal_draws <- rtnorm(n = 1e3, mu = mu, sigmas = list(s1, s2, s3))

# Example:
tic()
normal_result <- gof_test_eigenvalues(
  draws = normal_draws,
  model = "normal",
  seed = 123)
toc()

normal_result

skewt_draws <- rtskewt(n = 1e3, mu = mu,
                       sigmas = list(s1, s2, s3),
                       skew = array(rnorm(24), dim = c(2, 3, 4)))

# Fast eigenvalue version (no tensor bootstrap or repeated model fits):
gof_test_eigenvalues(draws = skewt_draws, model = "normal", seed = 123)
```

# Simple simulation study

This simulation checks three basic behaviors of the eigenvalue test:

1. Normal data should usually not be rejected by the normal model.
2. Skewed (t) data should often be rejected by the normal model.
3. Skewed (t) data should usually not be rejected by the skewed (t) model.

The first and third scenarios estimate the null rejection rate, which should be
near `alpha`. The second scenario estimates power and should have a larger
rejection rate. Because the fitted parameters are currently treated as known,
the null rejection rates are particularly important to inspect.

```{r simple-eigenvalue-simulation}
# Run a small simulation study for the eigenvalue GOF test.
simple_gof_simulation <- function(number_simulations = 25L,
                                  sample_size = 200L,
                                  alpha = 0.05,
                                  n_frequencies = 10L,
                                  n_mixture = 20000L,
                                  seed = 20260721,
                                  show_progress = TRUE) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # Parameters shared by the normal and skewed t distributions.
  mu <- matrix(c(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  sigmas <- list(
    matrix(c(1, 0.25, 0.25, 1.25), nrow = 2, ncol = 2),
    matrix(c(0.8, -0.15, -0.15, 1.1), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  )

  # These values create a moderately skewed, heavy-tailed alternative to the
  # tensor normal. Change them to investigate easier or harder alternatives.
  skew <- matrix(c(0.7, -0.35, 0.45, 0.2), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  nu <- 6

  scenario_names <- c(
    "normal data: test normal",
    "skewt data: test normal",
    "skewt data: test skewt"
  )

  # There are three test results for each simulation repetition.
  results <- data.frame(
    simulation = rep(seq_len(number_simulations), each = 3L),
    scenario = rep(scenario_names, times = number_simulations),
    p_value = NA_real_,
    reject = NA,
    expected_reject = rep(c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE),
                          times = number_simulations),
    correct_decision = NA
  )

  row_number <- 1L

  for (simulation in seq_len(number_simulations)) {
    if (show_progress) {
      message(
        "Simulation ", simulation, " of ", number_simulations
      )
    }

    normal_draws <- rtnorm(
      n = sample_size,
      mu = mu,
      sigmas = sigmas
    )

    skewt_draws <- rtskewt(
      n = sample_size,
      mu = mu,
      sigmas = sigmas,
      skew = skew,
      nu = nu
    )

    # Normal model applied to data generated from the normal model.
    normal_null <- tryCatch(
      gof_test_eigenvalues(
        draws = normal_draws,
        model = "normal",
        n_frequencies = n_frequencies,
        n_mixture = n_mixture,
        quiet = TRUE
      ),
      error = function(error) NULL
    )

    if (!is.null(normal_null)) {
      results$p_value[row_number] <- normal_null$p.value
    }
    row_number <- row_number + 1L

    # Normal model applied to skewed t data. Rejection is the desired outcome.
    normal_alternative <- tryCatch(
      gof_test_eigenvalues(
        draws = skewt_draws,
        model = "normal",
        n_frequencies = n_frequencies,
        n_mixture = n_mixture,
        quiet = TRUE
      ),
      error = function(error) NULL
    )

    if (!is.null(normal_alternative)) {
      results$p_value[row_number] <- normal_alternative$p.value
    }
    row_number <- row_number + 1L

    # Skewed t model applied to data generated from the skewed t model.
    skewt_null <- tryCatch(
      gof_test_eigenvalues(
        draws = skewt_draws,
        model = "skewt",
        n_frequencies = n_frequencies,
        n_mixture = n_mixture,
        quiet = TRUE
      ),
      error = function(error) NULL
    )

    if (!is.null(skewt_null)) {
      results$p_value[row_number] <- skewt_null$p.value
    }
    row_number <- row_number + 1L
  }

  results$reject <- results$p_value < alpha
  results$correct_decision <-
    results$reject == results$expected_reject

  # Summarize each scenario with explicit loops to keep the calculation easy
  # to inspect.
  summary <- data.frame(
    scenario = scenario_names,
    successful_fits = integer(length(scenario_names)),
    rejection_rate = numeric(length(scenario_names)),
    correct_decision_rate = numeric(length(scenario_names))
  )

  for (j in seq_along(scenario_names)) {
    rows <- results$scenario == scenario_names[j]
    successful <- rows & !is.na(results$p_value)

    summary$successful_fits[j] <- sum(successful)

    if (sum(successful) > 0L) {
      summary$rejection_rate[j] <- mean(results$reject[successful])
      summary$correct_decision_rate[j] <-
        mean(results$correct_decision[successful])
    } else {
      summary$rejection_rate[j] <- NA_real_
      summary$correct_decision_rate[j] <- NA_real_
    }
  }

  list(
    summary = summary,
    results = results,
    settings = list(
      number_simulations = number_simulations,
      sample_size = sample_size,
      alpha = alpha,
      n_frequencies = n_frequencies,
      n_mixture = n_mixture,
      mu = mu,
      sigmas = sigmas,
      skew = skew,
      nu = nu
    )
  )
}
```

Start with a small run to make sure everything behaves as expected. Increase
`number_simulations` to at least 500 when estimating a (5\%\) rejection rate
for a formal study.

```{r run-simple-eigenvalue-simulation, eval=FALSE}
simulation_result <- simple_gof_simulation(
  number_simulations = 25,
  sample_size = 200,
  seed = 123
)

simulation_result$summary

# Inspect all individual p-values and decisions if needed.
head(simulation_result$results)
```

For the two correctly specified scenarios, do not look only at the
`correct_decision_rate`: a test that never rejects would score highly by that
measure. Also check that the `rejection_rate` is reasonably close to `alpha`
and that the null p-values are spread across ([0,1]). Rejection rates near zero
together with p-values concentrated near one indicate that treating fitted
parameters as known is making the test conservative.

# Simulation study for the parameter-adjusted eigenvalue test

This version uses `compute_eigen_adjusted()` rather than the known-parameter
eigenvalues. The same fixed frequencies are used in every repetition and in
all scenarios. This makes changes in the results come from the simulated
samples rather than from selecting new frequencies for every test.

Each distribution is tested against its own fitted model to estimate Type I
error. Each skewed distribution is also tested against the tensor normal to
provide a simple power check. Correctly specified models should have rejection
rates near 0.05 and 0.10 in a large simulation; the misspecified normal models
should be rejected more often.

```{r adjusted-eigenvalue-simulation}
adjusted_eigenvalue_simulation <- function(
    number_simulations = 10L,
    sample_size = 300L,
    n_frequencies = 12L,
    n_mixture = 20000L,
    seed = 20260723,
    show_progress = TRUE) {

  set.seed(seed)

  # We use small 2 x 2 tensors so that a reasonably large simulation can be
  # completed quickly. The function itself works with other tensor dimensions.
  tensor_dims <- c(2, 2)
  p <- prod(tensor_dims)

  mu <- matrix(
    c(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1),
    nrow = 2,
    ncol = 2
  )

  sigmas <- list(
    matrix(c(
      1, 0.25,
      0.25, 1.25
    ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE),
    matrix(c(
      0.8, -0.15,
      -0.15, 1.1
    ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  )

  skew <- matrix(
    c(0.7, -0.35, 0.45, 0.2),
    nrow = 2,
    ncol = 2
  )

  nu <- 6
  gamma <- 3
  kappa <- 2
  lambda <- 2
  omega <- 3

  # Construct fixed reference frequencies at several radii. Each row is one
  # vectorized 2 x 2 frequency tensor.
  radii <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 3)
  frequencies <- matrix(
    0,
    nrow = n_frequencies,
    ncol = p
  )

  for (j in seq_len(n_frequencies)) {
    direction <- rnorm(p)
    direction <- direction / sqrt(sum(direction^2))

    radius_number <- ((j - 1L) %% length(radii)) + 1L
    frequencies[j, ] <- radii[radius_number] * direction
  }

  # Every distribution has one correctly specified null scenario. Each
  # skewed distribution also has a normal-model power scenario.
  data_models <- c(
    "normal",
    "skewt", "skewt",
    "vargamma", "vargamma",
    "invgauss", "invgauss",
    "genhyper", "genhyper"
  )

  fitted_models <- c(
    "normal",
    "normal", "skewt",
    "normal", "vargamma",
    "normal", "invgauss",
    "normal", "genhyper"
  )

  scenario_type <- c(
    "null",
    "alternative", "null",
    "alternative", "null",
    "alternative", "null",
    "alternative", "null"
  )

  scenario_names <- paste(
    data_models,
    "data: test",
    fitted_models
  )

  number_scenarios <- length(scenario_names)
  number_rows <- number_simulations * number_scenarios

  results <- data.frame(
    simulation = rep(
      seq_len(number_simulations),
      each = number_scenarios
    ),
    scenario = rep(
      scenario_names,
      times = number_simulations
    ),
    data_model = rep(
      data_models,
      times = number_simulations
    ),
    fitted_model = rep(
      fitted_models,
      times = number_simulations
    ),
    scenario_type = rep(
      scenario_type,
      times = number_simulations
    ),
    statistic = rep(NA_real_, number_rows),
    p_value = rep(NA_real_, number_rows),
    number_eigenvalues = rep(NA_integer_, number_rows),
    information_rank = rep(NA_integer_, number_rows),
    number_parameters = rep(NA_integer_, number_rows),
    failure = rep("", number_rows),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  # Carry out one adjusted eigenvalue test. This helper is kept inside the
  # simulation function because it is only needed for this study.
  one_adjusted_test <- function(current_draws, current_model) {

    current_fit <- tensor_mle(
      current_draws,
      model = current_model,
      max_iter = 1000L,
      tol = 1e-6,
      quiet = TRUE
    )

    # This is the same observed statistic used by gof_test_eigenvalues().
    observed <- .gof_cf_statistic(
      draws = current_draws,
      model = current_model,
      fit = current_fit,
      frequencies = frequencies
    )

    adjusted <- compute_eigen_adjusted(
      draws = current_draws,
      freqs = frequencies,
      model = current_model,
      fit = current_fit,
      return_details = TRUE
    )

    eigenvalues <- adjusted$eigenvalues

    # Simulate the inexpensive weighted chi-squared approximation.
    mixture_statistics <- numeric(n_mixture)

    for (j in seq_along(eigenvalues)) {
      mixture_statistics <- mixture_statistics +
        eigenvalues[j] * rchisq(n_mixture, df = 1)
    }

    p_value <- (
      1 + sum(mixture_statistics >= observed$statistic)
    ) / (
      n_mixture + 1
    )

    list(
      statistic = observed$statistic,
      p_value = p_value,
      number_eigenvalues = length(eigenvalues),
      information_rank = adjusted$information_rank,
      number_parameters = adjusted$number_parameters
    )
  }

  row_number <- 1L

  for (simulation in seq_len(number_simulations)) {

    if (show_progress) {
      message(
        "Adjusted-eigenvalue simulation ",
        simulation,
        " of ",
        number_simulations
      )
    }

    # Generate one sample from each distribution. When a sample is tested
    # against two models, both tests use exactly the same observations.
    generated_draws <- list(
      normal = rtnorm(
        n = sample_size,
        mu = mu,
        sigmas = sigmas
      ),
      skewt = rtskewt(
        n = sample_size,
        mu = mu,
        sigmas = sigmas,
        skew = skew,
        nu = nu
      ),
      vargamma = rtvargamma(
        n = sample_size,
        mu = mu,
        sigmas = sigmas,
        skew = skew,
        scale = gamma
      ),
      invgauss = rtinvgauss(
        n = sample_size,
        mu = mu,
        sigmas = sigmas,
        skew = skew,
        kappa = kappa
      ),
      genhyper = rtgenhyper(
        n = sample_size,
        mu = mu,
        sigmas = sigmas,
        skew = skew,
        lambda = lambda,
        omega = omega
      )
    )

    for (scenario in seq_len(number_scenarios)) {

      current_result <- tryCatch(
        one_adjusted_test(
          current_draws = generated_draws[[data_models[scenario]]],
          current_model = fitted_models[scenario]
        ),
        error = function(error) error
      )

      if (inherits(current_result, "error")) {
        results$failure[row_number] <-
          conditionMessage(current_result)
      } else {
        results$statistic[row_number] <-
          current_result$statistic
        results$p_value[row_number] <-
          current_result$p_value
        results$number_eigenvalues[row_number] <-
          current_result$number_eigenvalues
        results$information_rank[row_number] <-
          current_result$information_rank
        results$number_parameters[row_number] <-
          current_result$number_parameters
      }

      row_number <- row_number + 1L
    }
  }

  # Summarize the null rejection rates and power at both commonly used levels.
  summary <- data.frame(
    scenario = scenario_names,
    scenario_type = scenario_type,
    successful_tests = integer(number_scenarios),
    mean_p_value = numeric(number_scenarios),
    median_p_value = numeric(number_scenarios),
    rejection_rate_05 = numeric(number_scenarios),
    rejection_rate_10 = numeric(number_scenarios)
  )

  for (scenario in seq_len(number_scenarios)) {
    use_rows <-
      results$scenario == scenario_names[scenario] &
      is.finite(results$p_value)

    current_p_values <- results$p_value[use_rows]
    summary$successful_tests[scenario] <-
      length(current_p_values)

    if (length(current_p_values) == 0L) {
      summary$mean_p_value[scenario] <- NA_real_
      summary$median_p_value[scenario] <- NA_real_
      summary$rejection_rate_05[scenario] <- NA_real_
      summary$rejection_rate_10[scenario] <- NA_real_
    } else {
      summary$mean_p_value[scenario] <-
        mean(current_p_values)
      summary$median_p_value[scenario] <-
        median(current_p_values)
      summary$rejection_rate_05[scenario] <-
        mean(current_p_values <= 0.05)
      summary$rejection_rate_10[scenario] <-
        mean(current_p_values <= 0.10)
    }
  }

  list(
    summary = summary,
    results = results,
    frequencies = frequencies,
    settings = list(
      number_simulations = number_simulations,
      sample_size = sample_size,
      n_frequencies = n_frequencies,
      n_mixture = n_mixture,
      seed = seed,
      mu = mu,
      sigmas = sigmas,
      skew = skew,
      nu = nu,
      gamma = gamma,
      kappa = kappa,
      lambda = lambda,
      omega = omega
    )
  )
}
```

Start with a very small run to check the computation, then increase
`number_simulations`. A formal Type I error study should generally use at least
500 repetitions.

```{r}
univar_norm <- rnorm(1e3, mean = 2, sd = 4)

mean_est <- mean(univar_norm)
sd_est <- sd(univar_norm)

norm_cf <- function(t, mean, sd) {
  exp(1i * mean * t - 1/2 * sd^2 * t^2)
}

empirical_cf <- function(draws, t) {
  z <- complex(length(t))

  for (j in seq_along(t)) {
    z[j] <- mean(exp(1i * draws * t[j]))
  }

  z
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

B <- 2000
n <- length(univar_norm)

# Observed statistic
mean_est <- mean(univar_norm)
sd_est <- sd(univar_norm)

z_emp <- empirical_cf(univar_norm, t)
z_theory <- norm_cf(t, mean_est, sd_est)

# Use the same weight function as defined above
weight <- exp(-0.5 * t^2)

dt <- diff(t)[1]

T_obs <- n * sum(
  weight * Mod(z_emp - z_theory)^2
) * dt

# Bootstrap null distribution
T_boot <- numeric(B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  x_boot <- rnorm(
    n = n,
    mean = mean_est,
    sd = sd_est
  )

  # Re-estimate parameters within each bootstrap sample
  mean_boot <- mean(x_boot)
  sd_boot <- sd(x_boot)

  z_emp_boot <- empirical_cf(x_boot, t)
  z_theory_boot <- norm_cf(t, mean_boot, sd_boot)

  T_boot[b] <- n * sum(
    weight * Mod(z_emp_boot - z_theory_boot)^2
  ) * dt
}

#bootstrap p-value
mean(T_boot >= T_obs)
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

R <- 500
alpha <- 0.05
reject <- logical(R)

for (r in seq_len(R)) {
  # Example alternative: standardized t distribution
  x_alt <- as.numeric(scale(rt(n, df = 3)))

  mean_alt <- mean(x_alt)
  sd_alt <- sd(x_alt)

  z_emp_alt <- empirical_cf(x_alt, t)
  z_theory_alt <- norm_cf(t, mean_alt, sd_alt)

  T_alt <- n * sum(
    weight * Mod(z_emp_alt - z_theory_alt)^2
  ) * dt

  # Bootstrap null fitted to the alternative sample
  T_null <- numeric(B)

  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    x_boot <- rnorm(n, mean_alt, sd_alt)

    z_emp_boot <- empirical_cf(x_boot, t)
    z_theory_boot <- norm_cf(
      t, mean(x_boot), sd(x_boot)
    )

    T_null[b] <- n * sum(
      weight * Mod(z_emp_boot - z_theory_boot)^2
    ) * dt
  }

  p_alt <- mean(T_null >= T_alt)
  reject[r] <- p_alt < alpha
}

mean(reject)
```


# Goal

Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent tensor observations. At a frequency
vector \(t\), the empirical characteristic function (CF) is

\[
\widehat\varphi_n(t)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \exp\{i t^\top X_i\}.
\]

Its real and imaginary parts are sample averages of \(\cos(t^\top X_i)\)
and \(\sin(t^\top X_i)\). The fitted distribution supplies their theoretical
means and their joint covariance. Consequently, at a fixed set of \(L\)
frequencies, the CF differences can be treated like a vector of correlated
sample-mean differences.

Let \(d\) contain the real and imaginary CF differences at all frequencies,
and let \(V\) be their covariance under the null model. The test statistic is

\[
Q=n d^\top V^+ d,
\]

where \(V^+\) is a numerical pseudoinverse. When the model parameters are
fixed, the asymptotic null distribution is

\[
Q\ \overset{\cdot}{\sim}\ \chi^2_{\operatorname{rank}(V)}.
\]

The code below implements this test for the tensor-variate normal (TVN) and
the tensor-variate skewed \(t\). It avoids a full Kronecker covariance matrix
by whitening each tensor mode separately.

# Shared helpers

```{r cf-helpers}
# Apply mode-specific matrices to one tensor.
.mode_transform <- function(x, matrices) {
  for (k in seq_along(matrices)) {
    x <- n_prod(x, k, matrices[[k]])
  }
  x
}

# Return matrices W_k satisfying W_k Sigma_k W_k' = I.
.whitening_matrices <- function(sigmas) {
  lapply(sigmas, function(S) {
    S <- as.matrix(S)
    S <- (S + t(S)) / 2
    solve(t(chol(S)))
  })
}

# Center and modewise-whiten every tensor, returning an n by p matrix.
.standardize_tensor_sample <- function(draws, mu, sigmas) {
  n <- n_draws(draws)
  dims <- draw_shape(draws)
  p <- prod(dims)
  whitening <- .whitening_matrices(sigmas)
  z <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n, ncol = p)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    zi <- pull_draw(draws, i) - mu
    zi <- .mode_transform(zi, whitening)
    z[i, ] <- as.numeric(zi)
  }

  z
}

# The cosine/sine observations whose column means form the empirical CF.
.cf_features <- function(z, frequencies) {
  phase <- z %*% t(frequencies)
  cbind(cos(phase), sin(phase))
}

# Given a CF evaluator, calculate the exact mean vector and covariance matrix
# of [cos(t_1'X),...,cos(t_L'X),sin(t_1'X),...,sin(t_L'X)].
#
# `cf` must accept a matrix with one frequency per row and return one complex
# CF value per row.
.cf_feature_moments <- function(frequencies, cf) {
  L <- nrow(frequencies)
  phi <- cf(frequencies)

  if (length(phi) != L || any(!is.finite(phi))) {
    stop("The CF evaluator returned invalid values.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  feature_mean <- c(Re(phi), Im(phi))
  feature_second <- matrix(0, nrow = 2 * L, ncol = 2 * L)

  for (j in seq_len(L)) {
    for (k in seq_len(L)) {
      t_plus <- frequencies[j, ] + frequencies[k, ]
      t_j_minus_k <- frequencies[j, ] - frequencies[k, ]
      t_k_minus_j <- -t_j_minus_k

      phi_plus <- cf(matrix(t_plus, nrow = 1L))
      phi_j_minus_k <- cf(matrix(t_j_minus_k, nrow = 1L))
      phi_k_minus_j <- cf(matrix(t_k_minus_j, nrow = 1L))

      # Product-to-sum identities:
      # cos(A)cos(B) = {cos(A-B) + cos(A+B)}/2
      # sin(A)sin(B) = {cos(A-B) - cos(A+B)}/2
      # cos(A)sin(B) = {sin(B+A) + sin(B-A)}/2
      feature_second[j, k] <-
        0.5 * Re(phi_j_minus_k + phi_plus)

      feature_second[L + j, L + k] <-
        0.5 * Re(phi_j_minus_k - phi_plus)

      feature_second[j, L + k] <-
        0.5 * Im(phi_plus + phi_k_minus_j)

      feature_second[L + k, j] <- feature_second[j, L + k]
    }
  }

  feature_cov <- feature_second - tcrossprod(feature_mean)
  feature_cov <- (feature_cov + t(feature_cov)) / 2

  list(mean = feature_mean, covariance = feature_cov)
}

# Calculate d' V^+ d using only numerically positive eigenvalues of V.
.quadratic_form_pinv <- function(d, V, relative_tolerance = 1e-8) {
  eig <- eigen(V, symmetric = TRUE)
  cutoff <- max(eig$values, 0) * relative_tolerance
  keep <- eig$values > cutoff

  if (!any(keep)) {
    stop("The CF feature covariance has numerical rank zero.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  projected <- crossprod(eig$vectors[, keep, drop = FALSE], d)
  value <- sum(as.numeric(projected)^2 / eig$values[keep])

  list(value = value, rank = sum(keep), eigenvalues = eig$values)
}
```

# Model characteristic functions

After modewise whitening, the TVN target distribution is \(N_p(0,I_p)\), so

\[
\varphi_{N_p(0,I)}(t)=\exp(-\lVert t\rVert^2/2).
\]

For the package's skewed \(t\), the whitened representation is

\[
Z = W a + \sqrt{W}\,\varepsilon,
\qquad
W\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\nu/2,\nu/2),
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim N_p(0,I_p),
\]

where \(a\) is the modewise-whitened skew tensor. Conditional on \(W\),

\[
E\{\exp(i t^\top Z)\mid W\}
=
\exp\left\{W\left(i t^\top a-\frac{1}{2}\lVert t\rVert^2\right)\right\}.
\]

The skewed-\(t\) CF below integrates out \(W\) using a large, reusable set of
inverse-gamma quadrature draws. These are numerical integration values, not
estimates of the unobserved \(W_i\)'s that generated the data.

```{r model-cfs}
.standard_normal_cf <- function(frequencies) {
  values <- exp(-0.5 * rowSums(frequencies^2))
  as.complex(values)
}

.make_standard_skewt_cf <- function(whitened_skew, nu,
                                    n_mixing = 20000L,
                                    mixing_uniforms = NULL) {
  if (!is.numeric(nu) || length(nu) != 1L || !is.finite(nu) || nu <= 0) {
    stop("`nu` must be one positive finite number.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  if (is.null(mixing_uniforms)) {
    w_quadrature <- invgamma::rinvgamma(
      n = n_mixing,
      shape = nu / 2,
      rate = nu / 2
    )
  } else {
    if (!is.numeric(mixing_uniforms) || !length(mixing_uniforms) ||
        any(!is.finite(mixing_uniforms)) ||
        any(mixing_uniforms <= 0 | mixing_uniforms >= 1)) {
      stop("`mixing_uniforms` must contain values strictly between 0 and 1.",
           call. = FALSE)
    }

    # Reusing the uniforms gives every fitted nu the appropriate inverse-gamma
    # law while coupling the numerical CF integration across bootstrap samples.
    w_quadrature <- invgamma::qinvgamma(
      mixing_uniforms,
      shape = nu / 2,
      rate = nu / 2
    )
  }

  whitened_skew <- as.numeric(whitened_skew)

  function(frequencies) {
    frequencies <- as.matrix(frequencies)
    q <- rowSums(frequencies^2)
    ta <- drop(frequencies %*% whitened_skew)

    vapply(seq_len(nrow(frequencies)), function(j) {
      if (q[j] == 0 && ta[j] == 0) {
        return(1 + 0i)
      }

      mean(exp(w_quadrature * (1i * ta[j] - 0.5 * q[j])))
    }, FUN.VALUE = complex(1))
  }
}
```

# The test function

The default frequencies have independent \(N(0,1/p)\) entries. Thus their
expected squared norm is approximately one even when the vectorized tensor
dimension \(p\) is large. This avoids the near-zero kernel/CF behavior that
can occur when frequencies are too large in high dimension.

```{r test-function}
tensor_cf_wald_test <- function(draws,
                                model = c("normal", "skewt"),
                                fit = NULL,
                                frequencies = NULL,
                                n_frequencies = 10L,
                                frequency_sd = NULL,
                                n_mixing = 20000L,
                                mixing_uniforms = NULL,
                                max_iter = 1000L,
                                tol = 1e-6,
                                quiet = TRUE,
                                restrict = NULL) {
  model <- match.arg(model)

  if (!inherits(draws, "tensor")) {
    stop("`draws` must be a `tensor` object.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  n <- n_draws(draws)
  dims <- draw_shape(draws)
  p <- prod(dims)

  if (n < 2L) {
    stop("At least two tensor observations are required.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  parameters_estimated <- is.null(fit)

  if (parameters_estimated) {
    fit <- tensor_mle(
      draws,
      model = model,
      max_iter = max_iter,
      tol = tol,
      quiet = quiet,
      restrict = restrict
    )
  }

  required <- if (model == "normal") {
    c("mu", "sigmas")
  } else {
    c("mu", "sigmas", "skew", "nu")
  }

  missing_fit <- setdiff(required, names(fit))
  if (length(missing_fit)) {
    stop(
      "`fit` is missing: ", paste(missing_fit, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  if (is.null(frequencies)) {
    if (is.null(frequency_sd)) {
      frequency_sd <- 1 / sqrt(p)
    }

    frequencies <- matrix(
      stats::rnorm(n_frequencies * p, sd = frequency_sd),
      nrow = n_frequencies,
      ncol = p
    )
  } else {
    frequencies <- as.matrix(frequencies)

    if (ncol(frequencies) != p) {
      stop(
        "`frequencies` must have ", p, " columns for this tensor shape.",
        call. = FALSE
      )
    }
  }

  z <- .standardize_tensor_sample(draws, fit$mu, fit$sigmas)
  observed_features <- .cf_features(z, frequencies)
  observed_mean <- colMeans(observed_features)

  if (model == "normal") {
    cf <- .standard_normal_cf
  } else {
    whitening <- .whitening_matrices(fit$sigmas)
    whitened_skew <- .mode_transform(fit$skew, whitening)
    cf <- .make_standard_skewt_cf(
      whitened_skew = whitened_skew,
      nu = fit$nu,
      n_mixing = n_mixing,
      mixing_uniforms = mixing_uniforms
    )
  }

  null_moments <- .cf_feature_moments(frequencies, cf)
  difference <- observed_mean - null_moments$mean
  quadratic <- .quadratic_form_pinv(
    difference,
    null_moments$covariance
  )

  statistic <- n * quadratic$value
  df <- quadratic$rank
  p_value <- stats::pchisq(statistic, df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)

  method <- paste0(
    "Finite-frequency CF-Wald test for the tensor-variate ",
    if (model == "normal") "normal" else "skewed t"
  )

  if (parameters_estimated) {
    method <- paste0(method, " (plug-in parameter estimates)")
  }

  structure(
    list(
      statistic = c(Q = statistic),
      parameter = c(df = df),
      p.value = p_value,
      method = method,
      data.name = deparse(substitute(draws)),
      fit = fit,
      frequencies = frequencies,
      observed_cf = complex(
        real = observed_mean[seq_len(nrow(frequencies))],
        imaginary = observed_mean[nrow(frequencies) + seq_len(nrow(frequencies))]
      ),
      theoretical_cf = complex(
        real = null_moments$mean[seq_len(nrow(frequencies))],
        imaginary = null_moments$mean[
          nrow(frequencies) + seq_len(nrow(frequencies))
        ]
      ),
      difference = difference,
      feature_covariance = null_moments$covariance,
      covariance_eigenvalues = quadratic$eigenvalues,
      parameters_estimated = parameters_estimated
    ),
    class = "htest"
  )
}
```

# TVN example

Here the true parameters are supplied to demonstrate the fixed-parameter
version of the test. Setting `fit = NULL` instead asks the function to estimate
the TVN parameters with `tensor_mle()`.

```{r tvn-example}
set.seed(20260719)

normal_mu <- array(c(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1), dim = c(2, 2))
normal_sigmas <- list(
  matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.5), 2, 2),
  matrix(c(0.8, -0.2, -0.2, 1.2), 2, 2)
)

normal_draws <- rtnorm(
  n = 1000,
  mu = normal_mu,
  sigmas = normal_sigmas
)

normal_fixed_fit <- list(
  mu = normal_mu,
  sigmas = normal_sigmas
)

set.seed(1)
normal_test <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
  normal_draws,
  model = "normal",
  fit = normal_fixed_fit,
  n_frequencies = 10
)

normal_test
```

For real data, the call is:

```{r tvn-fitted-example, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(1)
normal_test_fitted <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
  observed_tensor_draws,
  model = "normal",
  n_frequencies = 10
)
```

# Tensor skewed-t example

The skewed-\(t\) example uses the same finite-frequency statistic, but its
theoretical CF and covariance are calculated by integrating over the fitted
inverse-gamma mixing distribution.

```{r skewt-example}
set.seed(20260719)

skewt_mu <- array(c(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1), dim = c(2, 2))
skewt_skew <- array(c(0.35, -0.15, 0.2, 0.1), dim = c(2, 2))
skewt_sigmas <- list(
  matrix(c(1, 0.2, 0.2, 1.3), 2, 2),
  matrix(c(0.9, -0.1, -0.1, 1.1), 2, 2)
)
skewt_nu <- 8

skewt_draws <- rtskewt(
  n = 1000,
  mu = skewt_mu,
  sigmas = skewt_sigmas,
  skew = skewt_skew,
  nu = skewt_nu
)

skewt_fixed_fit <- list(
  mu = skewt_mu,
  sigmas = skewt_sigmas,
  skew = skewt_skew,
  nu = skewt_nu
)

set.seed(2)
skewt_test <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
  skewt_draws,
  model = "skewt",
  fit = skewt_fixed_fit,
  n_frequencies = 10,
  n_mixing = 20000
)

skewt_test
```

For real data, estimate the parameters by omitting `fit`:

```{r skewt-fitted-example, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(2)
skewt_test_fitted <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
  observed_tensor_draws,
  model = "skewt",
  n_frequencies = 10,
  n_mixing = 20000,
  tol = 1e-5
)
```

# Inspecting the CF differences

The result retains the pointwise empirical and theoretical CF values. This is
useful because a single p-value does not show which frequencies disagree.

```{r cf-difference-plot}
cf_difference <- Mod(
  skewt_test$observed_cf - skewt_test$theoretical_cf
)

plot(
  cf_difference,
  type = "h",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Frequency number",
  ylab = "Absolute CF difference",
  main = "Tensor skewed-t CF discrepancies"
)
```

# Interpretation and current limitation

Large values of \(Q\), and therefore small chi-squared p-values, indicate that
the empirical CF differs from the model CF by more than expected from ordinary
sampling variation at the chosen frequencies. Failing to reject does not prove
that the model is correct; it says that this collection of CF features did not
find a detectable discrepancy.

The chi-squared reference distribution directly applies when `fit` contains
parameters fixed independently of `draws`. When `fit = NULL`, the same data are
used both to estimate the model and to test it. Fitting makes the empirical and
theoretical CFs artificially closer, so the chi-squared p-value is only a
**plug-in asymptotic diagnostic**. The parametric-bootstrap function below
calibrates the fitted-model statistic by repeating the estimation step in every
bootstrap sample. The `parameters_estimated` element records whether the Wald
test used fixed or fitted parameters.

Using the same fixed frequency matrix is important when comparing models or
repeating a simulation study. For example:

```{r shared-frequencies, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(100)
p <- prod(draw_shape(observed_tensor_draws))
shared_frequencies <- matrix(
  rnorm(10 * p, sd = 1 / sqrt(p)),
  nrow = 10,
  ncol = p
)

normal_result <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
  observed_tensor_draws,
  model = "normal",
  frequencies = shared_frequencies
)

skewt_result <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
  observed_tensor_draws,
  model = "skewt",
  frequencies = shared_frequencies
)
```

# GRABMyo tensor-model goodness-of-fit checks

The processed GRABMyo data contain 43 participant-level tensors, each with
dimensions $16\times28\times16$. Here we apply the characteristic-function
test only to the two tensor-variate models used in the main analysis: the
tensor normal and tensor skew-$t$.

```{r grabmyo-cf-gof, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
grabmyo_tensors <- readRDS("grabmyo_session1_tensors_16x28x16.rds")
grabmyo_array <- simplify2array(grabmyo_tensors)
grabmyo_draws <- as_tensor(grabmyo_array, obs = 4)

set.seed(20260722)
grabmyo_normal_cf <- gof_test_eigenvalues(
  grabmyo_draws,
  model = "normal",
  n_frequencies = 20,
  n_mixture = 100000,
  max_iter = 1000,
  tol = 1e-4,
  quiet = TRUE
)

set.seed(20260722)
grabmyo_skewt_cf <- gof_test_eigenvalues(
  grabmyo_draws,
  model = "skewt",
  n_frequencies = 20,
  n_mixture = 100000,
  max_iter = 1000,
  tol = 1e-4,
  quiet = TRUE
)

grabmyo_cf_results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Tensor normal", "Tensor skew-t"),
  Statistic = c(
    unname(grabmyo_normal_cf$statistic),
    unname(grabmyo_skewt_cf$statistic)
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    grabmyo_normal_cf$p.value,
    grabmyo_skewt_cf$p.value
  ),
  `Fitted nu` = c(NA, grabmyo_skewt_cf$fit$nu)
)

knitr::kable(grabmyo_cf_results, digits = 4)
```

Both p-values are large, so this characteristic-function diagnostic does not
reject either fitted tensor model at conventional significance levels. The
skew-$t$ model is therefore compatible with the GRABMyo data according to
this diagnostic, although the test does not establish that the model is true.
The skew-$t$ model also has the lower AIC and BIC from the likelihood-based
comparison.

This table uses the eigenvalue approximation, which treats the fitted
parameters as known and is therefore a fast plug-in diagnostic. The fully
parametric bootstrap below instead refits every simulated sample. Because a
skew-$t$ refit can encounter a numerical failure, the bootstrap result reports
both successful and failed replicates.

## Fully parametric bootstrap with refit failures recorded

The following version performs the full parametric bootstrap: it simulates
from the fitted model, refits that model to every bootstrap sample, and
recomputes the CF statistic. A failed refit is recorded rather than silently
discarded, so the stability of the numerical procedure is visible.

```{r cf-parametric-bootstrap-function}
tensor_cf_parametric_bootstrap <- function(draws,
                                           model = c("normal", "skewt"),
                                           fit = NULL,
                                           frequencies = NULL,
                                           B = 199L,
                                           n_frequencies = 10L,
                                           frequency_sd = NULL,
                                           n_mixing = 20000L,
                                           max_iter = 1000L,
                                           tol = 1e-6,
                                           quiet = TRUE,
                                           restrict = NULL,
                                           seed = NULL,
                                           show_progress = FALSE) {
  model <- match.arg(model)

  if (!inherits(draws, "tensor")) {
    stop("`draws` must be a `tensor` object.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (n_draws(draws) < 2L) {
    stop("At least two tensor draws are required.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (length(B) != 1L || !is.finite(B) || B < 1L || B != floor(B)) {
    stop("`B` must be one positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  B <- as.integer(B)
  if (!is.null(seed)) {
    set.seed(seed)
  }

  n <- n_draws(draws)
  p <- prod(draw_shape(draws))

  if (is.null(frequencies)) {
    if (is.null(frequency_sd)) {
      frequency_sd <- 1 / sqrt(p)
    }
    frequencies <- matrix(
      rnorm(n_frequencies * p, sd = frequency_sd),
      nrow = n_frequencies,
      ncol = p
    )
  } else {
    frequencies <- as.matrix(frequencies)
    if (ncol(frequencies) != p) {
      stop("`frequencies` must have ", p, " columns.", call. = FALSE)
    }
  }

  # Common uniforms reduce numerical-integration noise in comparisons between
  # the observed and bootstrap skew-t statistics. Each fitted nu transforms
  # them to its own inverse-gamma mixing distribution.
  mixing_uniforms <- if (model == "skewt") {
    runif(n_mixing)
  } else {
    NULL
  }

  if (is.null(fit)) {
    fit <- tensor_mle(
      draws,
      model = model,
      max_iter = max_iter,
      tol = tol,
      quiet = quiet,
      restrict = restrict
    )
  }

  observed <- tensor_cf_wald_test(
    draws,
    model = model,
    fit = fit,
    frequencies = frequencies,
    n_mixing = n_mixing,
    mixing_uniforms = mixing_uniforms,
    max_iter = max_iter,
    tol = tol,
    quiet = quiet,
    restrict = restrict
  )

  bootstrap_statistics <- rep(NA_real_, B)
  failures <- character(B)

  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    if (show_progress) {
      message("Bootstrap replicate ", b, " of ", B)
    }

    bootstrap_result <- tryCatch({
      bootstrap_draws <- if (model == "normal") {
        rtnorm(
          n = n,
          mu = fit$mu,
          sigmas = fit$sigmas
        )
      } else {
        rtskewt(
          n = n,
          mu = fit$mu,
          sigmas = fit$sigmas,
          skew = fit$skew,
          nu = fit$nu
        )
      }

      bootstrap_fit <- tensor_mle(
        bootstrap_draws,
        model = model,
        max_iter = max_iter,
        tol = tol,
        quiet = quiet,
        restrict = restrict
      )

      tensor_cf_wald_test(
        bootstrap_draws,
        model = model,
        fit = bootstrap_fit,
        frequencies = frequencies,
        n_mixing = n_mixing,
        mixing_uniforms = mixing_uniforms,
        max_iter = max_iter,
        tol = tol,
        quiet = quiet,
        restrict = restrict
      )
    }, error = function(error) error)

    if (inherits(bootstrap_result, "error")) {
      failures[b] <- conditionMessage(bootstrap_result)
      next
    }

    bootstrap_statistics[b] <- unname(bootstrap_result$statistic)
  }

  successful <- is.finite(bootstrap_statistics)
  if (!any(successful)) {
    stop("All bootstrap replicates failed.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  p_value <- (
    1 + sum(bootstrap_statistics[successful] >= unname(observed$statistic))
  ) / (1 + sum(successful))

  method <- paste0(
    "Parametric-bootstrap finite-frequency CF test for the tensor-variate ",
    if (model == "normal") "normal" else "skewed t"
  )

  structure(
    list(
      statistic = c(Q = unname(observed$statistic)),
      parameter = c(B = sum(successful)),
      p.value = p_value,
      method = method,
      data.name = deparse(substitute(draws)),
      fit = fit,
      frequencies = frequencies,
      observed_test = observed,
      bootstrap_statistics = bootstrap_statistics,
      B_requested = B,
      B_successful = sum(successful),
      B_failed = sum(!successful),
      failure_messages = failures[!successful]
    ),
    class = c("tensor_cf_bootstrap_test", "htest")
  )
}
```

# The examples use modest B while developing. Use B >= 999 for reported tests.
```{r simulated-parametric-bootstrap, eval=FALSE}
normal_boot <- tensor_cf_parametric_bootstrap(
  normal_draws,
  model = "normal",
  B = 999,
  n_frequencies = 10,
  seed = 20260722
)

skewt_boot <- tensor_cf_parametric_bootstrap(
  skewt_draws,
  model = "skewt",
  B = 999,
  n_frequencies = 10,
  n_mixing = 20000,
  seed = 20260722
)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Tensor normal", "Tensor skew-t"),
  Statistic = c(normal_boot$statistic, skewt_boot$statistic),
  `p-value` = c(normal_boot$p.value, skewt_boot$p.value),
  Successful = c(normal_boot$B_successful, skewt_boot$B_successful),
  Failed = c(normal_boot$B_failed, skewt_boot$B_failed)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

## Power sanity check with a deliberately wrong model

As a negative control, generate two compact and well-separated tensor-normal
populations, combine them into one bimodal sample, and fit a *single*
tensor-normal model. A single elliptical distribution cannot represent the two
clusters, so a useful CF test should reject it. This is a demonstration of
power against one conspicuous alternative, not a general power study.

```{r cf-bootstrap-power-check, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(20260725)

power_dims <- c(2, 2)
power_n_per_group <- 100L
power_sigmas <- list(diag(0.35, 2), diag(0.35, 2))

power_group_low <- rtnorm(
  n = power_n_per_group,
  mu = array(-2.5, dim = power_dims),
  sigmas = power_sigmas
)
power_group_high <- rtnorm(
  n = power_n_per_group,
  mu = array(2.5, dim = power_dims),
  sigmas = power_sigmas
)

# Combine the two tensor samples along their observation axis.
power_matrix <- rbind(
  matrix(unclass(power_group_low), nrow = power_n_per_group),
  matrix(unclass(power_group_high), nrow = power_n_per_group)
)
power_mixture_draws <- tensor(
  array(
    power_matrix,
    dim = c(2L * power_n_per_group, power_dims)
  ),
  obs = 1L
)

# B = 39 keeps this notebook check quick; its smallest possible add-one
# p-value is 1 / (39 + 1) = 0.025. Use a larger B for a reported analysis.
power_normal_boot <- tensor_cf_parametric_bootstrap(
  power_mixture_draws,
  model = "normal",
  B = 39,
  n_frequencies = 10,
  seed = 20260725
)

data.frame(
  Data = "Two-component bimodal tensor mixture",
  Fitted_model = "Single tensor normal",
  Statistic = unname(power_normal_boot$statistic),
  p_value = power_normal_boot$p.value,
  Successful = power_normal_boot$B_successful,
  Failed = power_normal_boot$B_failed,
  Decision_at_0.05 = ifelse(
    power_normal_boot$p.value < 0.05,
    "Reject",
    "Do not reject"
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)

hist(
  power_normal_boot$bootstrap_statistics,
  breaks = 12,
  main = "Power check: fitted tensor-normal null distribution",
  xlab = "Bootstrap CF-Wald statistic",
  col = "grey85",
  border = "white"
)
abline(
  v = unname(power_normal_boot$statistic),
  col = "firebrick",
  lwd = 2,
  lty = 2
)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = "Observed bimodal sample",
  col = "firebrick",
  lwd = 2,
  lty = 2,
  bty = "n"
)
```

With the fixed seed above, the observed statistic is about 335, whereas the
bootstrap statistics from a correctly specified single tensor-normal model
are below 23. The add-one bootstrap p-value is 0.025, so the negative-control
model is rejected at the 5% level. The p-value reaches the resolution limit
because this short demonstration uses only 39 bootstrap replicates.

For the GRABMyo tensors, the corresponding calls are:

```{r grabmyo-parametric-bootstrap, eval=FALSE}
grabmyo_normal_boot <- tensor_cf_parametric_bootstrap(
  grabmyo_draws,
  model = "normal",
  B = 999,
  n_frequencies = 20,
  seed = 20260722,
  show_progress = TRUE
)

grabmyo_skewt_boot <- tensor_cf_parametric_bootstrap(
  grabmyo_draws,
  model = "skewt",
  B = 999,
  n_frequencies = 20,
  n_mixing = 20000,
  seed = 20260722,
  show_progress = TRUE
)
```
